title: Beyond the Plain B-tree: Partial, Expression, Inverted and Block-Range Indexes
objectives: Use a partial index when queries only ever want a small slice of a table
Index a computed value such as lower(email) and know the query must match it
Pick an inverted index for words, tags and JSON keys, and a block-range index for append-only time data

cards.title: When a plain B-tree is the wrong shape
cards.body: A plain B-tree stores one entry for every row, keyed on the column exactly as stored. Four variations fix common mismatches. A partial index holds entries only for rows that match a condition, such as status = 'pending'. An expression index stores a computed value, such as lower(email), so a query on that expression can use it. An inverted index maps each element inside a value (a word, an array item, a JSON key) to the rows that contain it. A block-range index keeps only the smallest and largest value for each run of table pages. PostgreSQL offers all four; other engines cover some of them, for example SQL Server filtered indexes and MySQL functional key parts and full-text indexes.

cards.title: Worked example: a partial index for a job queue
cards.body: Workers keep asking for the oldest pending jobs. Almost every row in the table is finished work they never look at.
steps: Assume a jobs table of 50 million rows, of which about 5,000 are pending at any moment, and about 20 bytes per index entry (an estimate)
A full index on (status, created_at) holds 50 million entries: about 50,000,000 × 20 bytes ≈ 1 GB
A partial index on created_at WHERE status = 'pending' holds about 5,000 entries: about 100 KB, roughly a dozen 8 KB pages
The worker query WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 matches the index condition, so the planner can use it
When a job finishes, its new row version no longer matches the condition, so it adds no entry; the old entry is cleaned up with the dead row

cards.title: Expression indexes
cards.body: WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@example.com' cannot use a plain index on email, because the index is sorted by the stored value, not the lower-cased one. An index on lower(email) stores the computed value, so that exact expression becomes an index lookup. Made unique, it also stops 'Ann@x.com' and 'ann@x.com' from both being registered. Two rules apply. The query must use the same expression the index was built on, and the function must give the same result for the same input every time (PostgreSQL calls this immutable), or the index could hold stale answers. Each write pays for computing the expression once more.

cards.title: Inverted indexes for words, tags and JSON
cards.body: A B-tree on a whole array or document can only find rows whose entire value equals the search value. An inverted index flips the relationship around.
steps: Row 1 has tags {red, sale}, row 2 has {blue}, row 3 has {red}
The index stores each element once with the list of rows that contain it: red → 1, 3; sale → 1; blue → 2
“Rows tagged red” reads one short posting list instead of every row
Full-text search works the same way once text is split into normalised words
Writes cost more: one row can add dozens of entries, which is why PostgreSQL GIN can buffer new entries in a pending list

cards.title: Block-range indexes for naturally ordered data
cards.body: A block-range index (BRIN in PostgreSQL) stores one tiny summary per range of table pages, 128 pages by default: the minimum and maximum value found there. In an append-only events table, created_at rises with the physical position of rows, so a query for one day can skip every range whose minimum and maximum exclude that day. For a 100 GB table that is about 12 million pages, or roughly 95,000 summaries, a few megabytes in total, against several gigabytes for a B-tree on the same column. The price is precision: each matching range is read in full and rows are rechecked. And it only works while values follow physical order: a backfill of old rows or heavy updates that move rows widen the ranges until nothing can be skipped, so re-check EXPLAIN after bulk loads.

cards.title: Trap: a partial index the query does not match
cards.body: The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove from the query text that every row the query wants is inside the index. WHERE status = 'pending' matches an index built WHERE status = 'pending'. WHERE status IN ('pending', 'retry') does not, because retry rows are missing from it. A parameter can also hide the match: with a generic prepared plan, status = $1 could be any value, so the planner cannot assume it is 'pending'. Write the fixed condition literally in the query, and confirm the choice with EXPLAIN.

questions.prompt: A 40-million-row invoices table has about 2,000 rows with status 'unpaid'. A reminder job reads the unpaid rows by created_at every minute. Which index suits that job best?

choices.label: A B-tree on status that covers all 40 million rows
A partial index on created_at WHERE status = 'unpaid'
A hash index on the status column alone
A block-range index on the status column

questions.explanation: The partial index holds only the roughly 2,000 unpaid rows, so it stays tiny and cached, already sorted by created_at, and paid invoices never write to it. A full B-tree on status finds the same rows, but it is about 20,000 times larger and every invoice pays to maintain it. A hash index on status still has 40 million entries and cannot return rows in created_at order. A block-range index needs values that follow the physical row order, and status is scattered through the table.

questions.prompt: People sign in with any capitalisation of their email. You want WHERE lower(email) = lower(?) to be fast and 'Ann@x.com' to be rejected when 'ann@x.com' exists. Which change does both?

choices.label: A unique index on email, as the value is stored
A hash index on email plus a duplicate check in code
A unique index on the expression lower(email)
A partial index on email WHERE email IS NOT NULL

questions.explanation: An index on lower(email) stores the lower-cased value, so the lookup matches it and uniqueness applies to the lower-cased form. A unique index on the stored value treats 'Ann@x.com' and 'ann@x.com' as different, and lower(email) in the query cannot use it. A duplicate check in code races: two sign-ups can both pass the check before either inserts. Excluding NULL emails changes neither the case handling nor the lookup.

questions.prompt: A posts table stores tags as an array. Which index lets “posts tagged travel” avoid reading every row?

choices.label: A B-tree on the whole tags array value
A block-range index over the tags column
An expression index on the first tag only
An inverted index on the elements of tags

questions.explanation: An inverted index (GIN in PostgreSQL) keeps one list of rows per tag, so the search reads only the travel list. A B-tree on the array can only find posts whose entire tag list equals the one searched for. Tags are not ordered with the table's physical layout, so block-range summaries would match almost every range. Indexing only the first tag misses every post where travel comes second or later.

questions.prompt: Which table is the best fit for a block-range index on created_at?

choices.label: An append-only events log written in time order
A users table whose created_at values were backfilled at random
A lookup table of 200 country codes
A sessions table queried by exact session id

questions.explanation: In an append-only log, created_at rises with the physical position of rows, so each page range has a narrow minimum and maximum and most ranges can be skipped. Randomly backfilled values make each range span almost the whole time line, so almost nothing is skipped. A 200-row table fits in a page or two, so a scan is already cheap. Exact lookups by session id need an index on session id, not on created_at.

questions.prompt: A table occupies 6,400,000 pages of 8 KB. A block-range index keeps one summary per 128 pages. How many summaries does it hold?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: that is 50,000 summaries of a few dozen bytes each, a few megabytes for a table of about 52 GB (6,400,000 × 8 KB). A B-tree on the same column would have one entry per row and run to gigabytes. 6,400,000 would be one summary per page, and 800,000 comes from dividing by 8 instead of 128.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to replace a large full index with a partial one on a live table.

items.label: Confirm EXPLAIN now picks the partial index
Drop the old index once nothing uses it
Find the hot query and its fixed condition with EXPLAIN
Watch the usage statistics of the old index for a while
Create the partial index concurrently with exactly that condition

questions.explanation: The index condition must copy the query's condition, so you read the query first. You build the new index without blocking writes, then prove the planner uses it. Only after the old index shows no scans for a full business cycle (month-end jobs included) do you drop it. Dropping first would leave the hot query with no index at all.

questions.prompt: A shop with 2 million products needs search by words in product titles and descriptions. Products are edited about 50 times a second. What should it use first?
constraints: Search by any word, not only the first
Results in well under a second

approaches.label: LIKE '%word%' with a B-tree index on the text columns
A full-text inverted index on title and description
A separate search-engine cluster from day one

rationaleOptions.label: A B-tree speeds up LIKE when the pattern starts with %
Each word has its own list of rows, so a search reads only the matches
Databases cannot search for individual words inside text
Fifty edits a second is a modest write load for the extra index entries

rationaleConflicts.r3: A leading % gives the B-tree no prefix to seek on, so the database scans every row.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Most relational engines ship full-text indexing; PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server all do.

questions.explanation: An inverted full-text index answers word searches from posting lists, inside the database you already run. A separate search engine adds ranking features and scale, but also a second system to keep in sync; move to one when relevance tuning or load demands it, not before.

flashcards.back: Indexes only rows that match a condition; the query must imply that condition
Indexes a computed value such as lower(email); the query must use the same expression
Maps each word, array element or key to the rows containing it
Stores min and max per range of pages; tiny, but only useful when values follow physical order

mechanism.title: How each index type decides which entries to store
steps: A plain B-tree stores one entry per row: the column value exactly as stored, plus a pointer to the row. It answers equality, ranges and ordering on that value, and nothing else. Every variation below changes what is stored, so that a different question becomes a short lookup.

A partial index evaluates its condition on every write. Rows that fail the condition are not indexed at all, so a queue or an “unpaid” slice of a huge table keeps an index the size of the slice. At query time, the planner must prove that the query's WHERE clause implies the index condition, or it will not use the index.

An expression index computes a function of the row, such as lower(email) or (payload->>'country'), and indexes the result. It serves only queries that contain the same expression. Because stored results must stay valid, the function has to be deterministic: no current time, no random values, no session settings.

An inverted index splits each value into elements, such as words, array members or JSON keys, and keeps a posting list of row pointers for each element. Containment and word-match queries read one or a few posting lists and intersect them. One row can add many entries, so writes cost more, and PostgreSQL GIN can collect them in a pending list and merge them later.

A block-range index divides the table into runs of pages (128 by default in PostgreSQL) and stores a summary for each, usually the minimum and maximum value. A query reads only the runs whose summary could contain matches, then rechecks every row in them. It is tiny, but it helps only when values follow the physical order of rows.

In every case, confirm the planner's choice with EXPLAIN on real queries and real data, and drop indexes that never get used. Each extra index slows writes and takes memory away from the indexes that matter.

useWhen: A query always targets the same small slice of a large table: pending jobs, unpaid invoices, live rows under soft deletes
Queries filter on a computed value, such as case-insensitive email or a field inside a JSON document
You search inside values: words in text, tags in arrays, keys in documents
A huge append-only table is filtered by time and a B-tree on the timestamp would take gigabytes
avoidWhen: The condition changes from query to query, or arrives as a parameter, so no single partial index matches it
Values are scattered across the table, which makes block-range summaries overlap and skip nothing
The table is small, or the column is written far more often than it is searched
A plain B-tree already serves the query well; an extra index type adds write cost for no read gain

rows: Entries only for rows that match a condition
Queues, hot slices of big tables
The query must imply the condition
The query must repeat the exact expression
Min and max per run of pages

numbers.title: Sizing the job-queue index
assumptions: 50 million jobs, about 5,000 pending at any time
About 20 bytes per B-tree entry for a timestamp key, including overhead (an estimate)
steps: Full index: 50,000,000 × 20 bytes ≈ 1,000,000,000 bytes ≈ 1 GB.
Partial index: 5,000 × 20 bytes = 100,000 bytes ≈ 100 KB, which is about 100,000 ÷ 8,192 ≈ 12 pages.
Ratio: 5,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 0.01%, so the partial index is about 10,000 times smaller.
A finished job writes nothing to the partial index, while every row written to the table updates the full one.
numbers.result: A full (status, created_at) index finds pending jobs in a similar number of page reads, because they sit together in its leaves. The gain from the partial index is size, memory and write cost, not lookup depth.

india.title: PostgreSQL index documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual has separate chapters on partial indexes, indexes on expressions, GIN and BRIN. The partial index chapter explains that the planner uses such an index only when it can recognise that the query's WHERE condition implies the index predicate, and warns that parameterised conditions may defeat this. The BRIN chapter describes the page-range summaries, the default range of 128 pages, and why the index suits columns that correlate with physical row order. The GIN chapter covers posting lists and the pending-list fast-update option.

pitfalls.trap: Building a partial index and querying with a parameter
pitfalls.say: The planner cannot prove a parameter equals the index condition; write the fixed condition literally

pitfalls.trap: Using a function the database treats as non-deterministic in an expression index
pitfalls.say: The index needs a function whose result depends only on its input

pitfalls.trap: Assuming a block-range index still works after a random backfill
pitfalls.say: Out-of-order rows widen the ranges; check EXPLAIN after bulk loads

takeaways: Partial: index only the rows you query, then write that exact condition in the query
Expression: index the computed value and repeat the same expression in the WHERE clause
Inverted: for words, tags and JSON keys, at a higher write cost
Block-range: tiny summaries, useful only when values follow the physical order of rows

interactive.title: Will the planner use it?
interactive.prompt: Index: ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'unpaid'. Query: WHERE status IN ('unpaid', 'overdue') AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'. Can the planner answer this query from the partial index?

choices.label: Yes: status appears in the index condition
choices.feedback: Status appears, but the index lacks every overdue row, so using it would return incomplete results.

choices.label: No: the query also wants overdue rows, which the index does not contain
choices.feedback: Right: the query's condition does not imply the index condition, so the planner must use another path.

choices.label: Yes: created_at is the indexed column
choices.feedback: The column matches, but the index holds only unpaid rows, so overdue rows would be missed.

interactive.reveal: A partial index is usable only when the query's WHERE clause implies its condition. Either widen the index condition to status IN ('unpaid', 'overdue') or split the query in two.

EXPLAIN shows whether the planner actually picked your partial or expression index
Time-series storage, where block-range indexes and time partitions shine
Inverted indexes at search-engine scale, the next step after in-database full text

title: Choosing Primary Keys: Sequences, Random UUIDs and Time-Ordered IDs
objectives: Explain why random keys slow inserts once an index outgrows memory
Compare bigint sequences, UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 on locality, size, generation and exposure
Pick a key type for a given set of constraints

cards.title: The key decides where each insert lands
cards.body: A B-tree keeps its entries sorted by key. In engines that store rows inside the primary-key index (InnoDB, and SQL Server clustered indexes) the rows themselves sit in that order; in PostgreSQL the table is a heap, but the primary-key index is still sorted. A sequential id is always the largest so far, so every insert lands on the right-hand edge of the tree, and the same few leaf pages stay hot in memory. A random UUID (version 4) lands anywhere, so each insert touches a random leaf page somewhere in the index.

cards.title: Worked example: when the index outgrows memory
cards.body: Random keys cost almost nothing while the whole index fits in memory. The bill arrives when it no longer does.
steps: Assume a 40 GB primary-key index, 8 GB of memory caching its pages, and 2,000 inserts a second (illustrative)
Sequential keys: every insert goes to the rightmost leaf page, which is already cached
Random UUIDv4: the target leaf is cached with a probability of roughly 8 ÷ 40 = 20%
So about 80% of inserts read a page from storage first: 0.8 × 2,000 = 1,600 random reads a second
Those reads also evict pages other queries need, and random page splits leave pages emptier, so the index grows larger too

cards.title: Time-ordered UUIDs (version 7)
cards.body: UUID version 7, defined in RFC 9562 (2024), puts a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds in the leading bits and fills most of the rest with random bits. Keys created around the same time sort next to each other, so inserts cluster at the right edge of the index much as a sequence does. You keep the UUID benefits: any server or offline client can create one without asking the database, and the random part makes the next value impractical to guess. PostgreSQL 18 added a built-in uuidv7() function; elsewhere, generate them in the application or with a library.

cards.title: Size travels with the key
cards.body: A bigint is 8 bytes. A UUID stored in a native 16-byte type is 16 bytes. The same UUID stored as 36-character text takes 36 bytes or more and compares by text collation rules. The key is copied wherever it is referenced: every foreign key column in child tables, and every index on those columns. In InnoDB, every secondary index entry also stores the primary key, so a wider key enlarges every index on the table.

cards.title: Trap: sequential ids in public URLs
cards.body: If /invoices/1043 is a sequence value, anyone can try 1042 and 1044, and two invoices a week apart reveal how many you issue. Guessable ids are not a security hole on their own: the server must check that the caller owns invoice 1044 whatever the id looks like. But they make enumeration trivial and leak business volume. A common pattern keeps an internal bigint key for joins and adds a separate random or time-ordered public id with its own unique index.

cards.title: Edge case: time-ordered ids carry the time with them
cards.body: Anyone who sees a UUIDv7 can read when it was created, to the millisecond. For orders that rarely matters; for, say, an account id that should not reveal sign-up date, it might. Ordering also depends on clocks. Ids made on different machines sort only as well as those clocks agree, and a clock that jumps backwards can produce ids that sort before older ones. Treat the time order of ids as a storage convenience, not as the business order of events; keep an explicit timestamp or sequence where order matters.

questions.prompt: An insert-heavy table switched its primary key from a bigint sequence to random UUIDv4. Once the index grew past available memory, insert latency rose sharply. Why?

choices.label: Comparing 16-byte UUIDs costs far more CPU than integers
Each insert now lands on a random leaf page that is often not cached
The database scans the table for an existing equal UUID
Random keys stop the log from batching commits together

questions.explanation: Random keys spread inserts across the whole index, so once it is larger than memory most inserts must first read their leaf page from storage. Comparing 16-byte values is slightly slower than comparing 8-byte ones, but that cost is tiny and does not jump when the index outgrows memory. Uniqueness is checked with an index lookup, just as for a bigint, not with a table scan. Group commit batches log flushes the same way whatever the key values are.

questions.prompt: What makes UUID version 7 friendlier to a B-tree than version 4?

choices.label: It is shorter, so more keys fit on each page
It is created by the database, so values cannot collide
Its leading bits are a timestamp, so new keys sort near each other
It is stored as text, which compresses well inside pages

questions.explanation: Both versions are 128 bits; the difference is order. UUIDv7 starts with a millisecond timestamp, so recent keys share the hot right-hand edge of the index. It can be created anywhere, not only in the database, and collisions are avoided by its random bits, not by who creates it. Text storage makes any UUID larger, not friendlier.

questions.prompt: A table has 500 million rows and 4 secondary indexes in an engine where every secondary index entry stores the primary key, as InnoDB does. Switching the key from an 8-byte bigint to a 16-byte UUID adds how many GB of key bytes across those 4 secondary indexes?
assumptions: Each secondary entry stores the primary key
UUID is 8 bytes wider than bigint
questions.formula: rows × extra bytes per key × number of secondary indexes
questions.explanation: Sanity check: each secondary index grows by 500 million × 8 extra bytes = 4 GB, and there are 4 of them. The primary index and any child-table foreign keys grow on top of this. 4 GB counts only one index, and 32 GB uses the full 16 bytes instead of the 8-byte difference.

questions.prompt: An API serves /invoices/1043 using the table's sequence id. What is the realistic risk?

choices.label: A bigint sequence will run out of values within a few years
Integer ids make the index deeper than UUIDs would
Anyone can try neighbouring ids, and gaps reveal how many invoices you issue
Clients may cache an invoice under the wrong id

questions.explanation: Sequential ids are easy to enumerate and leak volume over time. Ownership checks are still required, but a separate random public id removes the easy guessing and the leak. A bigint sequence allows about 9.2 × 10^18 values, which does not run out at any realistic rate. A smaller 8-byte key gives a shallower or equal tree, not a deeper one. Caching by id works the same for any id type.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order for a random-key insert into an index larger than memory.

items.label: Insert the entry, splitting the leaf if it is full
Descend from the cached root to the leaf where the new key belongs
Later, a checkpoint writes the changed leaf back to storage
Evict a cold page and read that leaf from storage

questions.explanation: The upper levels are small and hot, so the descent is cheap; the leaf for a random key usually is not cached, so it is read from storage before it can be changed. The change is logged and the page is marked dirty, and a checkpoint or background writer flushes it later. With sequential keys the second step almost never happens.

questions.prompt: A new orders service: ids are created by several app servers and by mobile clients while offline, recent orders are read far more than old ones, and order ids appear in customer-facing URLs.
constraints: Ids created offline without the database
Inserts and recent reads stay fast at scale
Ids in URLs should not be guessable

approaches.label: A bigint sequence from the database, shown in URLs
A random UUIDv4 primary key
A UUIDv7 primary key created by the client or app server

rationaleOptions.label: Ids can be created offline without asking the database
Random keys spread inserts evenly, which a B-tree prefers
Recent orders sit together in the index, so inserts and recent reads stay cached
Sequence ids are safe to show because URLs are private

rationaleConflicts.r3: A B-tree prefers locality: spreading inserts across the index forces cache misses once it outgrows memory.
rationaleConflicts.r4: URLs end up in browser history, logs and shared links; neighbouring sequence ids are trivial to try.

questions.explanation: UUIDv7 meets all three constraints: no coordination, right-edge inserts and unguessable values. A sequence needs the database to create the id and is easy to enumerate; UUIDv4 is offline-friendly but scatters inserts. The cost is that ids reveal their creation time, which is acceptable for orders.

questions.prompt: Why is storing a UUID in a 36-character text column worse than using a native 16-byte type?

choices.label: Text columns cannot be indexed by a B-tree
It more than doubles the key size, and comparisons follow text collation rules
Text UUIDs lose their randomness once they are sorted
Text columns cannot be the target of a foreign key

questions.explanation: Every copy of the key, in indexes and child tables, is more than twice as large, and comparisons under a language collation are slower than comparing 16 raw bytes. Text can be indexed and referenced by foreign keys without problems, and sorting does not change how random the values are; the cost is purely size and comparison speed.

flashcards.back: Each insert touches a random leaf page; once the index outgrows memory, most inserts read from storage
RFC 9562 UUID with a millisecond timestamp first; sorts by creation time, created without coordination
Stores the primary key in every entry, so a wider key enlarges every index

mechanism.title: What a primary key choice changes underneath
steps: Every table needs a primary key that never changes. A generated surrogate key is the usual choice, because natural values such as email change. The open question is what kind of generated value to use, and the main options are a database sequence (bigint), a random UUID (version 4), and a time-ordered UUID (version 7) or similar time-first id.

The primary-key index is a B-tree sorted by key. With a sequence, each new key is the largest so far, so inserts always go to the rightmost leaf. That page and its parents stay in memory, and full pages split at the edge, leaving older pages almost full.

With a random key, the insert position is uniform across the index. While the index fits in memory this is cheap. Once it does not, the chance that the target leaf is cached is roughly memory ÷ index size, and every miss is a random read before the insert can finish. Splits happen in the middle of the tree, which leaves pages part empty, so the index is larger and fits memory even less.

A time-ordered key restores locality: its leading bits are a timestamp, so keys created in the same moment sit together at the right edge. It keeps the property that matters for distributed systems: any machine or offline client can create one without asking the database, and the random tail avoids collisions.

Width matters because the key is copied everywhere it is referenced: foreign key columns in child tables, their indexes and, in InnoDB, every secondary index of the table itself. Going from 8 to 16 bytes adds 8 bytes to each of those copies, and storing UUIDs as text roughly doubles that again.

Exposure is a separate decision. Sequence values leak volume and make enumeration trivial; time-ordered ids leak creation time; random ids leak nothing. Many systems use an internal bigint for joins and a separate public id, which keeps joins compact and URLs opaque.

useWhen: Use a bigint sequence when one database creates all ids and they are not shown to outsiders
Use UUIDv7 when ids must be created by many services or offline clients and the table is insert-heavy
Use an internal bigint plus a separate public id when you want compact joins and opaque URLs
Use a time-ordered id when recent rows are read far more than old ones
avoidWhen: Avoid random UUIDv4 as the primary key of a large, insert-heavy table that will outgrow memory
Avoid UUIDv7 where revealing an id's creation time is a problem
Avoid storing UUIDs as text when the engine has a native UUID or 16-byte binary type
Avoid using the time order of ids as the business order of events across machines

rows: Reveals time, not the next value

numbers.title: Cache misses from random keys
assumptions: 8 GB of memory available for its pages
steps: Chance a random leaf is cached ≈ 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2.
Misses per second ≈ (1 − 0.2) × 2,000 = 1,600 random reads.
At about 0.1 ms per SSD random read, that is 1,600 × 0.1 ms = 160 ms of storage time every second, before any query reads.
With sequential or time-ordered keys, the rightmost leaf is hot, so misses are close to zero.
numbers.result: The same insert rate costs about 1,600 extra storage reads a second with random keys and almost none with ordered ones, and the gap grows as the index grows.

india.title: RFC 9562 and the InnoDB index documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9562, published by the IETF in 2024, replaced RFC 4122 and defined UUID versions 6, 7 and 8. It describes version 7 as a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits, and recommends it over older versions for new database keys because it sorts by time. The MySQL manual explains that InnoDB stores rows in the clustered primary-key index and that every secondary index record contains the primary key columns, which is why it advises keeping the primary key short.

pitfalls.trap: Switching to UUIDv4 keys because ids must be created offline
pitfalls.say: Use UUIDv7: offline creation without scattering inserts

pitfalls.trap: Hiding sequence ids instead of checking ownership
pitfalls.say: Opaque ids reduce guessing; the server must still check that the caller owns the row

pitfalls.trap: Storing UUIDs as 36-character text
pitfalls.say: Use the native type: 16 bytes and fast comparisons

takeaways: Random keys scatter inserts; once the index outgrows memory most inserts read from storage
UUIDv7 is created anywhere and still sorts by time
The key is copied into every foreign key and, in InnoDB, every secondary index, so width matters
Exposure is its own decision: internal bigint plus public id is a common split

interactive.title: How often is the leaf already cached?
interactive.prompt: A primary-key index on random UUIDv4 keys is 60 GB. 15 GB of memory holds its pages, and inserts arrive at a steady rate. Roughly what share of inserts find their target leaf page already in memory?

choices.label: About 75%
choices.feedback: That is the miss rate: three quarters of the index is not in memory.

choices.label: Nearly all, as with a sequence
choices.feedback: A sequence keeps hitting the same hot page; random keys pick any leaf.

choices.label: About 25%
choices.feedback: Right: a uniformly random leaf is cached with a probability of about 15 ÷ 60.

interactive.reveal: With random keys, the cache hit chance for inserts is about memory ÷ index size, so it keeps falling as the table grows. Ordered keys keep it near 100% at any size.

title: Storing Trees in Tables: Adjacency Lists, Recursive Queries, Paths and Closure Tables
objectives: Store a hierarchy with parent_id and read a subtree in one recursive query
Compare materialised paths and closure tables on reads, moves and storage
Guard against cycles when rows can be moved

cards.title: Comments, folders and org charts
cards.body: Comment threads, folders, product categories and reporting lines are all trees, but a table is a flat list of rows. You choose how to encode the tree. Four encodings cover most needs: an adjacency list, where each row stores its parent_id; a recursive query that walks that list; a materialised path, where each row stores its full path such as /1/4/9/; and a closure table, with one row for every ancestor and descendant pair. They trade cheap moves against cheap reads.

cards.title: Adjacency list plus a recursive query
cards.body: An adjacency list is a parent_id column that references the same table. It is the simplest design to keep correct: moving a whole subtree is one update of one row, and a foreign key stops a parent from pointing at nothing. Reading a subtree means walking down level by level. A recursive common table expression (WITH RECURSIVE in PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0 and later, and SQLite; plain WITH in SQL Server) does that walk inside the database: an anchor query picks the start row, and a recursive part joins children to the rows found so far until no new rows appear. Index parent_id, because every level is a join on it.

cards.title: Worked example: loading a comment thread
cards.body: The tree design decides how many round trips a page needs. Round trips, not joins, usually dominate.
steps: Assume a thread of 1,000 comments, 6 levels deep, and 2 ms per database round trip (illustrative)
Children of each comment, one query per comment: 1,000 round trips ≈ 2 s, the N+1 pattern
One query per level from the application: 6 round trips ≈ 12 ms, plus code to stitch the levels together
One recursive query: 1 round trip; the database performs the 6 join steps internally
If threads are always loaded whole, a thread_id on every comment needs no recursion at all: fetch WHERE thread_id = ? and build the tree in memory

cards.title: Materialised paths and closure tables
cards.body: Both store extra data so that reads need no recursion. They differ in what a move costs.
steps: Materialised path: comment 9 under 4 under 1 stores path /1/4/9/
Subtree of 4: WHERE path LIKE '/1/4/%', a prefix scan on a B-tree (with a collation or operator class that supports prefix matching)
Moving 4 under another parent rewrites the path of every row beneath it
Closure table: one row (ancestor, descendant, depth) for every pair, including each node paired with itself at depth 0
Subtree or ancestors is one indexed lookup; a node inserted at depth d adds d + 1 rows

cards.title: Trap: a cycle in the data
cards.body: A foreign key on parent_id checks only that the parent exists. It does not stop a move that makes a folder its own ancestor: move A under B while B is already inside A, and the data now loops. A recursive query with UNION ALL then keeps going round A, B, A, B until it hits a depth limit or runs out of memory. Guard the move itself: inside the same transaction, check that the new parent is not a descendant of the node being moved. Add a depth limit or a cycle check to recursive queries as a second line of defence; PostgreSQL 14 and later have a CYCLE clause for this.

cards.title: Edge case: closure tables on deep trees
cards.body: A closure table stores depth + 1 rows per node, so its size depends on how deep the tree is. A bushy tree of a million categories, around 6 levels deep, needs about 7 million rows. A degenerate chain, such as a reply chain where each comment answers the previous one, is far worse: 10,000 comments in a single line need 10,000 × 10,001 ÷ 2 ≈ 50 million rows. Moving a subtree also rewrites every pair that crosses the move. Use closure tables for shallow, read-heavy trees such as categories, not for unbounded reply chains.

questions.prompt: A folders table stores parent_id. A user drags a folder that contains 3,000 descendants into another folder. How many rows change?

choices.label: All 3,001, because each descendant's ancestry changes
Two: the old parent and the new parent
One: the moved folder's parent_id
None, because the tree is rebuilt when it is read

questions.explanation: In an adjacency list each row knows only its direct parent, so the descendants still point at the same parents and only the moved folder changes. Ancestry is derived when you read, which is why reads need recursion. Parents store nothing about their children, so they do not change either. A materialised path would rewrite all 3,001 rows, and a closure table every pair that crosses the move.

questions.prompt: With an adjacency list, you need every descendant of category 12, at any depth, in one round trip. What do you write?

choices.label: A single self-join of categories on parent_id
A recursive common table expression that starts at category 12
A GROUP BY parent_id with a count of children
An index on parent_id and a plain SELECT for category 12

questions.explanation: The anchor selects category 12, and the recursive part repeatedly joins children to the rows found so far, so any depth is reached in one statement. A single self-join reaches only direct children, and each extra level needs another join written by hand. Grouping counts children but does not walk the levels. The index makes each recursive step fast, but a plain SELECT still returns only one level.

questions.prompt: Each comment stores a path such as /1/4/9/. Which operation becomes expensive?

choices.label: Listing every comment under comment 4
Finding the ancestors of comment 9
Inserting a new reply under comment 9
Moving comment 4 and its replies under another comment

questions.explanation: A move changes the path prefix of every row in the subtree, so a large subtree means a large rewrite. Listing a subtree is a prefix search on path. Ancestors can be read straight out of the path itself. A new reply copies its parent's path and appends its own id, which is one insert.

questions.prompt: A closure table stores one row per ancestor and descendant pair, including each node paired with itself. A new node is inserted at depth 5, where the root is depth 0. How many closure rows does that insert add?
assumptions: The new node is at depth 5
Each node is paired with itself
questions.formula: number of ancestors + 1 for the self-pair = depth + 1
questions.workedAnswer: The node has 5 ancestors (depths 0 to 4) plus itself: 5 + 1 = 6 rows
questions.explanation: Sanity check: one row for each ancestor at depths 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, and one for the node itself. Answering 5 forgets the self-pair, which many queries rely on to include the node in its own subtree.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order a recursive query follows to read a subtree.

items.label: Stop when a step finds no new rows
Join the rows found in the last step to their children by parent_id
Return all accumulated rows to the outer query
Run the anchor part, which selects the starting node
Add the new rows to the result and use them as the next step's input

questions.explanation: The anchor runs once. The recursive part runs repeatedly, each time only on the rows the previous step added, until a step adds nothing. With a cycle in the data that point never comes, which is why a cycle check or depth limit matters.

questions.prompt: A product catalogue has 5,000 categories, at most 6 levels deep. Pages show breadcrumbs (all ancestors) and “all products in this category and below”. Categories are reorganised a few times a year.
constraints: Breadcrumbs and subtree listings on every page view

approaches.label: Store the whole tree as one JSON document in a settings row
An adjacency list read with recursive queries
Copy each ancestor into fixed columns level1_id to level6_id on every product

rationaleOptions.label: With 5,000 categories, a recursive walk of 6 levels takes a few milliseconds
One JSON document is easier to keep correct under concurrent edits
A reorganisation is a single parent_id update per moved category
Fixed level columns adapt to any future depth

rationaleConflicts.r3: Six columns cap the depth at six, and every reorganisation rewrites the copied ancestors on every affected product.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Every edit rewrites the whole document, so two concurrent edits can overwrite each other unless you lock it.

questions.explanation: The tree is small and changes rarely, so the simplest correct design wins: parent_id with a foreign key and an index, read recursively. If profiling later shows the recursive reads are hot, cache the result or add a closure table then.

flashcards.back: Each row stores parent_id; moves are one update, subtree reads need recursion
Each row stores /1/4/9/; subtree is a prefix search, moves rewrite the subtree
One row per ancestor and descendant pair; reads are one lookup, depth + 1 rows per node

mechanism.title: How each tree encoding answers the three common questions
steps: Every tree design has to answer three questions: what are the children or descendants of this node, what are its ancestors, and what does it cost to move a subtree. A flat table answers none of them directly, so each design stores something extra or does extra work at read time.

An adjacency list stores only parent_id. Children are one indexed lookup. Descendants and ancestors require walking the tree one level per step, which a recursive common table expression does inside the database in one round trip. A move is one row. This is the default for good reason: it is hard to corrupt and easy to understand.

A recursive query has an anchor part that picks the starting rows and a recursive part that joins the rows found in the previous step to their children (or parents). It repeats until a step adds no rows, then returns everything. Each step is an indexed join on parent_id, so a tree of depth d costs about d small index scans.

A materialised path stores the chain of ancestor ids in each row. Descendants become a prefix search, ancestors can be parsed from the path, and depth is the number of separators. The price is moves: every row under the moved node gets a new prefix. PostgreSQL's ltree extension implements this pattern with its own operators and index support.

A closure table stores every ancestor and descendant pair, with depth, in a separate table. Descendants, ancestors and “is X under Y” are all one indexed lookup, with no recursion. Inserting a node at depth d adds d + 1 rows, and a move deletes and re-inserts every pair crossing the moved boundary, so it fits shallow, read-heavy trees.

Whatever the encoding, guard moves against cycles in the same transaction as the move, index the columns that reads walk on, and question whether you need a tree query at all: if a page always loads a whole thread, a thread_id column and an in-memory build are simpler than any of these.

useWhen: Use an adjacency list with recursive queries as the default for most trees
Use a materialised path when subtree reads are hot and moves are rare
Use a closure table for shallow, read-heavy trees that need ancestor and descendant checks
Use a plain thread_id when the application always loads the whole tree at once
avoidWhen: Avoid closure tables for unbounded chains such as long reply threads
Avoid materialised paths when large subtrees move often
Avoid walking a tree with one query per node from the application
Avoid fixed level1 to levelN columns when the depth can change

numbers.title: Round trips for a 1,000-comment thread
steps: One query per comment: 1,000 × 2 ms = 2,000 ms.
One query per level: 6 × 2 ms = 12 ms.
One recursive query: 1 × 2 ms = 2 ms of round trip, plus a few milliseconds of indexed joins inside the database.
Closure table for the same thread: about 1,000 × (average depth + 1) rows; at an average depth of 3, about 4,000 rows.
numbers.result: Moving the walk into one recursive query takes the page from about 2 seconds to a few milliseconds without changing the schema.

india.title: The PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server CTE documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: All three manuals document recursive common table expressions with tree-walking examples. The PostgreSQL chapter on WITH queries explains how the recursive part is evaluated using a working table until it is empty, and documents the SEARCH and CYCLE clauses for depth-first or breadth-first order and cycle detection. The MySQL manual describes recursion depth limits through cte_max_recursion_depth. The ltree page shows a materialised path type with ancestor and descendant operators.

pitfalls.trap: Writing a recursive query without a depth limit or cycle check
pitfalls.say: Bad moves create cycles; check moves, and bound the recursion

pitfalls.trap: Indexing nothing but the primary key
pitfalls.say: Every recursive step joins on parent_id; index it

pitfalls.trap: Choosing a closure table for reply chains
pitfalls.say: Rows grow with depth; long chains explode the table

takeaways: Adjacency list plus a recursive query is the default: one-row moves, one round trip reads
Materialised paths make subtree reads a prefix search but moves rewrite the subtree
Closure tables make every tree question one lookup at depth + 1 rows per node
Check moves for cycles; a foreign key alone does not prevent them

interactive.title: What happens after a bad move?
interactive.prompt: Folder A contains folder B. A bug moves A under B, so A's parent is B and B's parent is A. A recursive query that uses UNION ALL and tracks depth now lists A's subtree. What happens?

choices.label: The foreign key rejected the move, so nothing changes
choices.feedback: Both folders exist, so the foreign key is satisfied; it checks existence, not cycles.

choices.label: It returns A and B once each
choices.feedback: UNION ALL keeps every row, and the depth column makes each pass different, so nothing stops repetition.

choices.label: It loops A, B, A, B until a depth limit or memory runs out
choices.feedback: Right: each step finds the other folder again as a child, forever.

interactive.reveal: Prevent cycles where they start, by checking in the move transaction that the new parent is not a descendant, and bound recursive queries with a depth limit or a CYCLE clause.

seeAlso.why: The N+1 query problem is what walking a tree one node at a time turns into
Joins, since every recursive step is a join of rows to their children
Indexes on parent_id and path are what make each tree step cheap

title: Table Partitioning and Data Retention
objectives: Split one large table into partitions and know how it differs from sharding
Write queries that let the planner skip partitions
Replace large retention deletes with dropping whole partitions

cards.title: One table name, many physical pieces
cards.body: Declarative partitioning splits a table into child tables, called partitions, by a partition key: most often time ranges, such as one partition per day or month, sometimes a list of values or a hash. Applications still read and write the parent table name, and the database routes each row to its partition. All partitions live on the same database server. That is the difference from sharding, which spreads data across machines to add capacity. Partitioning makes one big table easier to manage, prune and expire.

cards.title: Worked example: deleting 90-day-old events
cards.body: Retention is the clearest win, because deleting rows and dropping files cost very different amounts.
steps: Assume 20 million events a day, kept for 90 days: 20,000,000 × 90 = 1.8 billion rows (illustrative)
Without partitions, each night DELETE WHERE created_at < now() - 90 days removes 20 million rows one by one, writing log records, index changes and dead row versions
Vacuum or purge must then clean those 20 million dead rows, and the table keeps the freed space as bloat
With daily partitions, the job detaches and drops the oldest day's partition
Dropping a partition removes its files in one catalog operation, whatever its size, and leaves no dead rows behind

cards.title: Pruning: skipping partitions
cards.body: When a query's WHERE clause constrains the partition key, for example created_at >= '2026-10-01', the planner skips every partition that cannot hold matching rows. With constant values it prunes while planning; with parameters, PostgreSQL can also prune when the query runs. A query that does not mention the key has nothing to prune on, so it must visit every partition. With 36 monthly partitions, a lookup by customer_id becomes 36 index probes instead of one.

cards.title: Choosing the partition key
cards.body: Choose a key that appears in most queries' filters and matches how data ages: time for events, logs and orders; region or tenant lists where data is managed per customer. Uniqueness follows the partitions. In PostgreSQL, a primary key or unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key columns, because each partition enforces uniqueness only within itself. A rule that order_id alone is unique across all partitions needs another mechanism, such as a sequence or UUID that cannot repeat.

cards.title: Trap: thousands of tiny partitions
cards.body: Each partition is a real table with its own files, indexes and statistics. Planning time and lock overhead grow with the number of partitions a query might touch, and memory use grows with the total. Hourly partitions kept for two years means 17,520 tables. Size partitions so typical queries touch a handful, and keep the total in the hundreds or low thousands; daily or monthly is usually enough.

cards.title: Edge case: a row with nowhere to go
cards.body: If an insert arrives with a timestamp beyond the last partition, PostgreSQL rejects it because no partition matches. A default partition catches such rows, but has its own cost: creating a partition for a range later requires checking that the default holds no rows for that range, and moving any it does. Create partitions ahead of time with a scheduled job, alert when anything lands in the default partition, and treat a full default partition as a bug.

questions.prompt: An events table keeps 30 days of data. The nightly DELETE of the oldest day takes an hour and leaves the table bloated. What fixes it best?

choices.label: Add an index on created_at so the DELETE finds rows faster
Run VACUUM FULL right after each nightly DELETE
Partition by day and drop the oldest partition each night
Run the DELETE as one larger transaction once a week

questions.explanation: Dropping a partition removes a whole day's files at once, with no per-row log records and no dead rows to clean up. An index helps find rows, but the cost is writing millions of deletions. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table under an exclusive lock, blocking all access while it runs. A weekly delete is seven times bigger, with longer locks and more bloat in one go.

questions.prompt: An orders table is partitioned by month on created_at. Which query can the planner answer from a single partition?

choices.label: WHERE customer_id = 7 AND total > 100 AND total < 500
WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id = 7 AND total > 0
WHERE total > 100 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'

questions.explanation: Only the query that bounds created_at lets the planner rule out every month but September. Filters on customer_id, status or total say nothing about which month a row is in, so every partition must be searched. Ordering by created_at does not filter rows, so it does not prune either.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, why must a unique constraint on a partitioned table include the partition key?

choices.label: Each partition enforces uniqueness only within itself
The partition key is always the primary key
Indexes on partitions can only hold a single column
The planner needs it to choose a partition on insert

questions.explanation: Indexes are built per partition, so a value can be checked only against its own partition. Including the partition key ensures equal values land in the same partition, where the check can see them. The partition key is often not the primary key at all, partition indexes can have many columns, and routing an insert uses the partition key value itself, not a unique constraint.

questions.prompt: A team creates hourly partitions and keeps them for 2 years. How many partitions exist?
questions.explanation: Design implication: that is far beyond the hundreds or low thousands that keep planning and memory overhead low. Daily partitions for the same two years would be 730. 8,760 counts only one year, and 730 is the daily count.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a monthly partition rotation in order.

items.label: Copy the detached partition to cheap storage if it must be kept
Create next month's partition ahead of time
Drop the detached partition
Detach the partition that has passed the retention window
New rows route to it automatically when the month starts

questions.explanation: Creating partitions ahead avoids rejected inserts at the month boundary. Detaching first removes the old partition from queries without deleting it, so it can be archived safely; only then is it dropped. Dropping before archiving loses the data for good.

questions.prompt: A 4 TB orders table runs on one server whose CPU sits at about 30%. Queries mostly filter by month, and orders older than five years must be moved to cold storage each year.

approaches.label: Keep one table and add more indexes
Shard across eight servers by customer id
Range-partition by month on the same server

rationaleOptions.label: Sharding becomes necessary once a table passes 1 TB
Month filters let the planner skip all but one or two partitions
More indexes make yearly archiving cheaper
Archiving becomes detaching whole partitions

rationaleConflicts.r3: Size alone does not demand sharding; this server has spare CPU, and sharding adds cross-shard queries and operations.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Indexes add write and storage cost and do nothing to make moving old rows cheaper.

questions.explanation: The server has capacity, so the problem is managing one big table, which is exactly what partitioning solves. Shard when one machine can no longer carry the load, not before.

flashcards.back: Partitioning splits a table on one server; sharding spreads data across servers
The planner skips partitions when the WHERE clause constrains the partition key
Detach and drop the oldest partition instead of deleting rows

sources.title: SQL Server: Partitioned tables and indexes

mechanism.title: How a partitioned table routes, prunes and expires data
steps: A partitioned table is a parent with no rows of its own and a set of child tables. Each child accepts a slice of the partition key: a range such as one month, a list such as a set of regions, or a hash bucket. Every row lives in exactly one partition.

On insert, the database evaluates the partition key and routes the row to the matching partition. If none matches and there is no default partition, the insert fails. Updates that change the key move the row from one partition to another, which costs a delete plus an insert.

On read, the planner compares the WHERE clause with each partition's bounds and removes partitions that cannot match. That is pruning. It happens while planning for constants, and in PostgreSQL also during execution for parameters and join values. Queries without the key search every partition.

Indexes are created on each partition separately. That keeps each index small, so it stays in memory, but it means uniqueness is checked per partition; in PostgreSQL a unique constraint must include the partition key columns.

Retention becomes a metadata operation. Detaching a partition removes it from the parent so queries stop seeing it, and dropping it deletes its files. No row-by-row log records, no dead rows and no vacuum or purge work follow.

All of this stays on one server. Partitioning helps manage a big table, keep indexes small, and make archiving cheap; it does not add CPU, memory or disk. When one machine cannot carry the load, sharding is the next step, and a time-partitioned table is often easier to shard later.

useWhen: A large table is filtered by time in most queries
Old data must be deleted or archived on a schedule
Indexes on one huge table no longer fit in memory, but recent partitions' indexes would
Bulk loads should land in a fresh partition and be attached when complete
avoidWhen: The table is small enough that a plain index already serves every query
Most queries do not filter on any candidate partition key
You need a unique rule that cannot include the partition key, without an id that already guarantees it
You need more CPU or storage than one server has; that is sharding

rows: DELETE row by row, then vacuum
Goes to one shard if the key is the shard key

numbers.title: Nightly retention, with and without partitions
steps: Total rows kept: 20,000,000 × 90 = 1.8 billion.
Without partitions: 20 million row deletions a night, each with log and index work, then 20 million dead rows to clean.
With daily partitions: 90 live partitions plus one being created ahead, and 1 drop a night.
Compare hourly partitions: 24 × 90 = 2,160 live partitions, more planning work for little extra benefit at this size.
numbers.result: Daily partitions turn a 20-million-row delete into one drop and keep the partition count near 90.

india.title: PostgreSQL partitioning chapter
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual's table partitioning chapter covers range, list and hash partitioning, explains partition pruning at plan and execution time, and lists the limitations, including that unique and primary key constraints on a partitioned table must include all partition key columns. It also recommends dropping or detaching partitions for bulk removal instead of large DELETE statements, and warns that too many partitions increase planning time and memory use.

pitfalls.trap: Partitioning on a key that queries do not filter by
pitfalls.say: Every query then probes every partition; choose the key from the queries

pitfalls.trap: Creating partitions only when the first row arrives
pitfalls.say: Create them ahead with a scheduled job, and alert on the default partition

pitfalls.trap: Expecting partitioning to add capacity
pitfalls.say: It stays on one server; shard when one machine is not enough

takeaways: Partitioning splits a table on one server; sharding spreads it across servers
Queries must filter on the partition key for pruning to work
Retention becomes detach and drop instead of deleting millions of rows
Keep partitions few enough that planning and memory overhead stay small

interactive.title: Which partitions does this query read?
interactive.prompt: orders is partitioned by month for 36 months, and each partition has an index on customer_id. A query runs WHERE customer_id = 7. What does the database do?

choices.label: It reads only the newest partition
choices.feedback: Nothing in the query says the rows are recent, so the planner cannot assume that.

choices.label: It rejects the query because created_at is missing
choices.feedback: Queries without the key are allowed; they just cannot be pruned.

choices.label: It probes the customer_id index in all 36 partitions
choices.feedback: Right: without the partition key there is nothing to prune on.

interactive.reveal: A query without the partition key costs one index probe per partition. If customer lookups dominate, add a time bound to them, or reconsider the partition key.
